After one year, the average temperature would be around minus seventy-three degrees.
Picture a city on a wide river, under a great suspension bridge.
The river would be frozen solid at the top, a road of ice from bank to bank.
Deep below, the water would still be liquid, kept from freezing by Earth's own inner heat.
Near hot springs on the ocean floor, tiny life could carry on, never needing the Sun at all.
But every bridge and every tower around you was built for a world warmed by the Sun.
In this cold, ordinary steel turns brittle, almost like glass.
And the cold makes it shrink, pulling every cable tighter.
For a while, it would hold.
The bridge would creak and groan in the dark.
Every week, a little colder than the last.
Then, one cable snaps.
The deck tilts.
One by one, the others follow.
And Earth itself would no longer circle anything.
Without the Sun's pull, it would fly off in a straight line, about thirty kilometers every second.
Every day, more than two and a half million kilometers farther from where the Sun used to be.
The stars would be brighter than you have ever seen them.
Every bit of warmth you have ever felt came from one star.
And it would never come back.
